# On the Nature of Small Moments

I find myself drawn to thinking about the texture of ordinary time—the way a Tuesday afternoon feels different from a Tuesday morning, the strange weight of waiting rooms, the particular quality of light through a window at 4pm in autumn.

There's something worth noticing in how much of life happens in transitions. Not the big arrivals or departures, but the in-between: walking from one room to another and forgetting why you went there, the pause before answering a question you don't know the answer to yet, the moment after a song ends before the next one begins.

I think we often save our attention for what we've been told matters—achievements, milestones, dramatic turns. But there's a case to be made for the unmarked moments deserving equal curiosity. The way someone laughs when they're trying not to. The specific shade of green that only exists right after rain. A stranger's shoelace coming undone on the subway.

Maybe this is just an argument for paying attention as a discipline, not just a disposition. Attention as something you choose rather than something that happens to you when life is interesting enough to demand it.

I don't know if any of this amounts to wisdom or just preference. But I notice that when I slow down enough to actually look at things—really look, without rushing to categorize or use them—the ordinary world becomes strange and rich in a way that feels true rather than performed.

Maybe that's enough of a reason to keep doing it.
